topics.title: Brahman and the deities
topics.source: From Finn's workbook (10 Sept “Hindu beliefs about God”: one God or many?; 11 Sept: the Sanskrit word for God; 13 Nov starter: Brahman, Trimurti, deities, murti; the Key Words page) and his notes. The questions are ours.
topics.summary: Hindus believe in one God, Brahman, who is shown through many deities. The Trimurti are the three deities for the three things God does: create, preserve, destroy.

images.caption: The Trimurti: three deities showing three things Brahman, the one God, does.

table.title: The Trimurti (“three forms”)
head: Deity
Role
Look out for
rows: Four heads, the Vedas, a swan
The preserver — keeps the universe safe and in balance
The destroyer — destroys so new things can be created

facts: **Brahman** is the one ultimate reality — God. It is the word for God in **Sanskrit**, the ancient language of the Hindu holy books. Hindus believe Brahman is everywhere and in everything.
Brahman is too great for people to understand all at once, so Hindus worship Brahman through **deities** (gods and goddesses).
A **deity** is a form that represents one part of God — like the different faces of one person. So most Hindus believe in **one God shown in many forms**.

**One God or many?** (the class question, 10 Sept) It can look as if Hindus believe in many gods, because they worship many deities. But most Hindus believe there is **one God, Brahman**, and the deities are all forms of Brahman. A good answer says both.
Deities are often shown with **many heads or arms** to show that they are **superhuman** beings — more powerful than any human.
A **murti** is a statue or image of a deity. Hindus use murtis to help them focus on God when they worship (puja).

The **Trimurti** means “three forms”: **Brahma** the creator, **Vishnu** the preserver and **Shiva** the destroyer. Together they show the never-ending cycle of the universe: created, kept going, destroyed, created again.
Each deity's picture is full of **symbols**: what they hold, wear or ride all tell you something about them.
An **avatar** is a form Vishnu takes when he comes down to Earth to fight evil, such as **Rama** and **Krishna**.
The **atman** is the soul. Hindus believe a part of Brahman is in every living thing.
**Om** (Aum) is the sacred sound and symbol of Brahman, said at the start of prayers.
keywords: a form representing a part of God (a god or goddess)
a statue or image of a deity
“three forms” of God: Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva
a form Vishnu takes on Earth, e.g. Rama, Krishna
the soul — part of Brahman in every living thing

topics.title: Karma, rebirth and moksha
topics.source: From Finn's workbook: “Key beliefs – karma and rebirth” (11 Sept), the starters on 8 and 9 Oct (karma, moksha, samsara, reincarnation, atman), 12 Nov and the Key Words page. The class definitions are kept; the questions are ours.
topics.summary: Hindus believe the soul (atman) is reborn again and again (samsara). Karma — your actions, thoughts and intentions — shapes your future. The goal is moksha: release from the cycle.

table.title: The key words (class definitions)
head: Key word
Meaning
rows: Actions, thoughts and intentions shape your future
The cycle of life, death and rebirth

facts: **Karma**: Hindus believe your **actions, thoughts and intentions shape your future** — all actions in life have **consequences**. Good karma brings good results, bad karma bad results, in this life or the next.
The **atman** is the **soul or spirit**. Hindus believe it never dies.
For Hindus, **death is not the end**: the atman is **reborn into another body** (**reincarnation**). Good karma can lead to a better next life.
**Samsara** is the **cycle of life, death and rebirth** that the atman goes round again and again.
**Moksha** means **liberation, freedom or release** — the atman is freed from samsara and joins Brahman. It is the final goal for Hindus.
**Watch the mix-up:** samsara is the **cycle**; moksha is the **escape** from the cycle. (Memory hook: **M**oksha = **M**ade free.)
**How karma changes a life:** someone who believes in karma tries to do good actions — and think good thoughts — so there are good consequences, and avoids harming others.
keywords: actions, thoughts and intentions shape your future
the cycle of life, death and rebirth
liberation, freedom or release from samsara

topics.title: Brahma, the creator
topics.source: From Finn's homework (24 Sept): his labelled picture of Brahma — the meanings in the table are the ones he wrote. Picture redrawn; extra notes and questions are ours.
topics.summary: Brahma created the universe. Learn what his four heads, the Vedas, the water pot, the prayer beads, the lotus and the swan stand for.

images.caption: Brahma and his symbols. Hide the names and test yourself.

head: Symbol
What it means
rows: Four heads (only three seen — one faces backwards)

facts: **Brahma** is the **creator**: he made the universe and everything in it.
Hindus tell that Brahma was **born from a lotus** growing out of Vishnu's navel.

He has **four heads**, facing the four directions — he sees and knows everything. In pictures you can **only see three**: the fourth faces backwards. The four **Vedas** (the oldest holy books) are said to have come from his four mouths.
He holds the **Vedas**, a **water pot**, **prayer beads** and a **lotus**, and rides a **swan**.
His wife is **Saraswati**, goddess of knowledge and learning.
Brahma is **rarely worshipped**: there are very few temples to him. One story says it is because his work — creating — is finished.

topics.title: Vishnu, the preserver
topics.source: From Finn's homework (24 Sept): his labelled picture of Vishnu (“Good homework Finn”) — the discus, conch, mace and lotus meanings are the ones he wrote. Picture redrawn (his shows Vishnu standing); extra notes and questions are ours.
topics.summary: Vishnu keeps the universe safe and comes to Earth as avatars to defeat evil. Learn what his blue skin, four arms, discus, conch, mace and lotus mean.

table.title: Vishnu's symbols
head: Symbol
What it means
rows: The sound of creation and spiritual awakening
Like the sky and ocean: endless, everywhere

facts: **Vishnu** is the **preserver**: he keeps the universe safe and in balance, and protects good against evil.
When evil grows strong, Vishnu comes down to Earth as an **avatar**. Hindus tell of ten avatars, including **Rama**, **Krishna** and **Narasimha** (half man, half lion — see Holika and Prahlad).
His **blue skin** is the colour of the sky and the ocean, which seem endless: Vishnu is infinite and everywhere.
His **four arms** show he is all-powerful. He holds the **Sudarshana chakra** (a discus), a **conch shell**, a mace called **Kaumodaki** and a **lotus**.
He is often shown **standing on a pedestal**, called a **peetham** (or a lotus pedestal, padmapitha).
He rides **Garuda**, an eagle, and is often shown resting on the great snake **Shesha** in the cosmic ocean.
His wife is **Lakshmi**, goddess of wealth and good fortune.
Hindus who see Vishnu as the most important deity follow **Vaishnavism**.

topics.summary: Shiva destroys so that new things can be made, and destroys evil and ignorance. Learn the meaning of his third eye, raised hand, snake, tiger skin, trident, drum, moon and the river Ganges.

head: Symbol

facts: Shiva is a **male deity** and one of the **principal (main) gods** of Hinduism.
**Shiva** is the **destroyer**. Destroying is not just bad: old things must end so **new things can be created**. He also destroys evil and ignorance.
He has a **third eye** (**trinetra**) of wisdom; when it opens, it destroys evil.
He holds a **trident (trishul)** and a small **drum (damaru)**, and wears a **snake** round his neck — a sign of **bravery**. His raised hand is a symbol of **peace**.
He sits on (and wears) a **tiger skin**: he is the **master of his own mind**.
A **crescent moon** sits in his hair, and the **River Ganges** flows from it: Shiva caught the falling river in his hair so it would not flood the Earth.
His **blue throat** comes from a story where he drank a poison to save the world.
As **Nataraja**, Lord of the Dance, he dances inside a ring of fire, ending one universe so a new one can begin.
He meditates on **Mount Kailash** in the Himalayas, rides the bull **Nandi**, and his wife is **Parvati**. Their son is **Ganesha**.
Hindus who see Shiva as the most important deity follow **Shaivism**.

topics.title: Holy books: Shruti and Smriti
topics.source: From Finn's workbook: 8 Oct (Shruti “heard and seen”: the V…, the U…; Smriti “remembered”: the R…, the P…, the M…, the L… of M…), the 9 Oct starter and the Key Words page. The blanks are filled in here; the questions are ours.
topics.summary: Hindu holy books come in two groups: Shruti (“heard”) — the Vedas and Upanishads — and Smriti (“remembered”) — the Ramayana, the Puranas, the Mahabharata and the Laws of Manu.

table.title: The two groups of holy books
head: Group
Means
The books
rows: The Ramayana · The Puranas · The Mahabharata · The Laws of Manu

facts: Hindu holy books (scriptures) are in **Sanskrit**, an ancient language, and come in two groups.

**Shruti** means “**heard**” (and seen). Hindus believe these were **revealed by God** to wise men (rishis) long ago, who heard them. They are the **most important**: the **Vedas** (the oldest holy books) and the **Upanishads** (teachings about Brahman and the atman).

**Smriti** means “**remembered**”. These were **remembered and passed on by people**, then written down: the **Ramayana** (the story of Rama and Sita), the **Puranas** (stories of the deities), the **Mahabharata** (a great war story — it includes the **Bhagavad Gita**) and the **Laws of Manu** (rules for living, including the four stages of life).
Memory hook: **Sh**ruti — “**sh**h, listen!” (heard). **Sm**riti — “**s**o **m**emorable” (remembered).
**Smartism** takes its name from Smriti: Smartas are followers of Smriti.
keywords: “heard” — revealed scriptures: the Vedas, the Upanishads
“remembered” — the Ramayana, Puranas, Mahabharata, Laws of Manu

the ancient language of the holy books

topics.title: Holika and Prahlad
topics.source: From Finn's workbook (storyboard of Holika and Prahlad, Oct) and “Hinduism homework 2” (22 Oct, questions a–d, copied into his book): how the story teaches about good and evil, devotion, blessings and being led into bad things. Story retold and questions are ours.
topics.summary: The story behind the festival of Holi: Prahlad stays devoted to Vishnu, his aunt Holika is burned, and Vishnu as Narasimha defeats the demon king. What does it teach Hindus?

table.title: What the story teaches (the homework questions)
head: The lesson
In the story
rows: Holika burns but Prahlad is safe; Narasimha defeats the demon king. Holi bonfires remember it.
b) Devotion to God is rewarded
Prahlad keeps praying to Vishnu, and Vishnu protects him every time.
c) Use your blessings the right way
Holika's gift (safe from fire) was meant for good; she used it to kill, so it failed her. The king misused his boon too.
d) People can be led into doing bad things
Holika did evil because her brother told her to — she followed him instead of doing right.

facts: **Hiranyakashipu** was a proud demon king. He had a **boon** (a blessing) that he could not be killed by man or animal, inside or outside, by day or by night, on the ground or in the sky, by any weapon. He thought he could not die, and ordered everyone to **worship him instead of God**.
His son **Prahlad** refused: he stayed **devoted to Vishnu** and kept praying to him.
The king tried to kill Prahlad many times (snakes, elephants, a cliff), but **Vishnu protected him** every time.
The king's sister **Holika** had a **gift that kept her safe from fire** (often a magic shawl). She sat in a bonfire holding Prahlad on her lap to burn him.
Because she **misused her gift** for evil, it failed her: the shawl flew to Prahlad. **Holika burned, and Prahlad was safe.**

Then Vishnu came as **Narasimha**, half man and half lion, and defeated the king **at dusk** (not day or night), **in a doorway** (not inside or outside), **on his lap** (not ground or sky), **with his claws** (no weapon) — so the boon was not broken.
Hindus remember the story at **Holi**: bonfires on the night before (**Holika Dahan**) show good beating evil; the next day people throw **coloured powder** and water and celebrate spring.

Vishnu's avatar: half man, half lion
deep love and loyalty to God

topics.title: The four stages of life
topics.source: From Finn's workbook: “The four stages of life in Hinduism” (Nov), the matching starter (karma, Smriti, Shruti, Holika, Holi) and the Key Words page (ashrama). Notes and questions are ours.
topics.summary: The four ashramas (stages of a Hindu life): Brahmacharya the student, Grihastha the householder, Vanaprastha retirement, and Sannyasa, giving everything up to focus on moksha.

table.title: The four ashramas
head: Stage
Name
What happens
rows: The student stage: learn the scriptures from a teacher (guru), self-control
The householder stage: marry, work, raise a family, give to others
The retirement stage: hand over to the children, more time for prayer
Give up belongings and put all attention on moksha

facts: An **ashrama** is a **stage of life**. Hindu teaching (the **Laws of Manu**) describes **four stages of life**, traditionally for **Hindu men**.
**Brahmacharya — the student stage**: a young person learns the scriptures from a teacher (**guru**) and learns self-control.
**Grihastha — the householder stage**: marrying, working, earning money and raising a family; looking after others and giving to charity. It is their **dharma** (duty) to their family and society.
**Vanaprastha — the retirement stage**: when the children are grown up, the person hands over the household, gives advice and spends more time on prayer and spiritual things.
**Sannyasa**: the person **gives up their belongings** (and family ties) and puts **all their attention on moksha**. Today few people take this stage.
Memory hook, in order: **B**right **G**rown-ups **V**ery **S**ensibly — Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha, Sannyasa.
keywords: one of the four stages of a Hindu life
giving up belongings to focus on moksha

topics.title: Four Hindu traditions
topics.source: From Finn's notes (the table of Vaishnavism, Shaivism, Shaktism and Smartism) and his workbook, “Different groups of Hindus” (13 Nov). Questions are ours.
topics.summary: Hindus belong to different traditions depending on which deity they see as most important: Vishnu, Shiva, the Goddess, or five deities as equals.

table.title: The four main traditions
head: Tradition
Who they worship
Key beliefs
Their worship
rows: Vishnu (and his avatars Rama and Krishna) as the most important deity
Shiva, as the most important deity and creator
Shiva is within and part of this world
The Goddess is the ultimate reality
Worshipping the Goddess, e.g. as Durga or Kali
Five deities as equals (Shiva, Vishnu, Devi, Ganesha, Surya); follows the Smriti scriptures
All five are forms of the one Brahman

facts: Hinduism has several **traditions** (denominations). They share many beliefs, but differ in **which deity they see as most important**.

**Vaishnavism**: Vishnu (and his avatars, Rama and Krishna) is the most important deity. Followers show **devotion** to Vishnu; their worship uses **holy books** and honours **many saints**. It is the biggest tradition.
**Shaivism**: Shiva is the most important deity — and the creator. They believe Shiva is **within and part of this world**. Their worship includes **puja and yoga**.
**Shaktism**: worship of **Devi**, the **Mother Goddess** (Shakti, divine power), as the ultimate reality — for example as **Durga** or **Kali**.
**Smartism**: follows the **Smriti** scriptures and worships **five deities** — Shiva, Vishnu, Devi, Ganesha and Surya (the sun) — as equal forms of Brahman; each person chooses one to focus on.

**What the names mean** (workbook, 13 Nov): **Vaishnavite** means a **worshipper of Vishnu**, who they see as the most important deity and the creator. **Shaivites** practise **yoga to discipline their mind and body** in their goal to reach **moksha**. **Shaktism** means the teaching of **energy, power, the goddess** — Shaktas worship **Devi**. **Smartism** means a **follower of Smriti** (the “remembered” scriptures).
keywords: worship of Vishnu as the most important deity
worship of Shiva as the most important deity
worship of Devi, the Mother Goddess
five deities worshipped as equal forms of Brahman
deep love and loyalty to God (bhakti)

topics.title: Ganesha, remover of obstacles (extra)
topics.source: Our notes: one of the main Hindu deities with a symbol picture (not from a class sheet we've seen). Picture is ours.
topics.summary: Ganesha, the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati, removes obstacles and is prayed to before anything new. Learn what his head, ears, tusk, belly, axe, rope, sweets and mouse mean.

table.title: Ganesha's symbols
head: Symbol
What it means
rows: Sacrifice; keep the good, throw away the bad
Take in everything life brings, good and bad
Cut away bad habits and obstacles
Pull people closer to God and their goals
The reward of a good life

facts: **Ganesha** (Ganesh) is the **remover of obstacles** and the god of **new beginnings** and **wisdom**.
Hindus pray to Ganesha **before starting something new** — a journey, an exam, a wedding, a new business.
He is the son of **Shiva and Parvati**. The story: Parvati made Ganesha to guard her door; Shiva, not knowing him, cut off his head; to make things right, Shiva gave him the head of an elephant.
His **elephant head** stands for wisdom, his **big ears** for listening, his **big belly** for taking in all of life, good and bad.
His **broken tusk**: he broke it off to write down the long holy story the **Mahabharata** — a sign of sacrifice.
He holds an **axe**, a **rope (noose)** and **sweets (modaks)**, and rides a **mouse**.
keywords: something in the way that stops you
a long Hindu holy story Ganesha wrote down

topics.title: Lakshmi, goddess of wealth (extra)
topics.source: Our notes: one of the main Hindu deities with a symbol picture (not from a class sheet we've seen). Picture is ours.
topics.summary: Lakshmi, Vishnu's wife, is the goddess of wealth and good fortune, welcomed into homes at Diwali. Learn what her lotus flowers, gold coins, elephants and four arms mean.
facts: **Lakshmi** is the goddess of **wealth, good fortune and beauty**. She is the wife of **Vishnu**.
She sits or stands on a **lotus** and holds lotus flowers: purity and beauty.
**Gold coins** pour from her hand: she brings wealth and good fortune to those who work hard and are devoted.
Two **elephants** pour water over her: royalty, and the rain that brings good harvests.
Her **four arms** stand for the four aims of life: duty (dharma), wealth (artha), happiness (kama) and freedom from rebirth (moksha).
At **Diwali**, the festival of lights, Hindus light lamps (divas) and clean their homes to welcome Lakshmi in.
keywords: goddess of wealth and good fortune, Vishnu's wife
the festival of lights, when Lakshmi is welcomed

topics.title: Worship (extra)
topics.source: Extra: worship key words often in Year 7 Hinduism tests (puja, mandir, aarti, dharma, ahimsa), not in Finn's workbook. Ours. Karma, samsara and moksha are in “Karma, rebirth and moksha”.
topics.summary: How Hindus worship: puja at home and in the mandir, aarti, offerings — plus dharma (duty) and ahimsa (not harming).
facts: **Puja** is worship. Many Hindus do puja every day at a **shrine at home**, as well as at the **mandir** (temple).
In puja, Hindus make offerings to the **murti** — flowers, fruit, sweets, water, incense — and ring a bell.
In **aarti**, a tray with a flame (lamp) is waved in circles in front of the murti; worshippers pass their hands over the flame and then over their heads to receive God's blessing.
**Dharma** is your duty — doing the right thing in your life.
**Ahimsa** means not harming any living thing; it is why many Hindus are vegetarian.
keywords: worship with a flame waved before the murti
a special place for worship, often at home
